2. The suit, Title Suit No. 137 of 1989 instituted on 12-4-89 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Bagerhat was for a declaration that the registered deed No. 4464 of 1984 dated 15-9-84 in favour of the defendant-appellants is void and not binding upon the plaintiff-respondent and also for permanent injunction restraining them from entering into Bashbaria Gher, an area of 85 acres of land earmarked for shrimp cultivation. The plaintiff's case was that a deed was registered by the owners on 7-10-87 giving permission to the plaintiff to cultivate shrimp in that area for 7 years from 1394 B.S. to 1400 B.S., at a meeting of the owners at the office of defendant No. 3, Rampal Upazila Parishad Chairman. Upon application dated 10-10-87 defendant No. 3 granted license in favour of the plaintiff to cultivate shrimp, being No. 15 dated 7-3-88 valid upto 31-12-88. This license was renewed upto 31-12-89 on 13-2-89. The plaintiff thereafter constructed sluice gate, canals etc. and took other steps to cultivate shrimp in the Gher. The plaintiff later on came to know that a deed dated 15-4-84 was executed in favour of the appellants in collusion with the Chairman of the Union Parishad concerned. The appellants were now trying to dispossess the plaintiff from the Gher and hence the suit as also the application for temporary injunction. 

 3. The learned Assistant Judge issued show cause notice and granted an order of ad-interim injunction on 12-4-89. The appellants, showing cause, contended that they were owners of more than 50 acres out of 85 acres. The appellants obtained earlier consent from the other owners of the remaining 35 acres and also obtained permission from them to cultivate shrimp in the area by an earlier registered deed dated 15-4-84. The applicants were inducted in possession on the basis of the aforesaid deed and the plaintiff has no possession of the same. 

 4. After hearing the parties the trial Court by an order dated 6-6-89 vacated the order of ad-interim injunction and disallowed the prayer for temporary injunction, but the lower appellate Court set aside the order and granted temporary injunction. The main argument of the appellate Court below was that while the plaintiff had both a registered deed and a license from 1987, the appellants had an earlier registered deed in their favour, but no license before 2-4-89 and as such the plaintiff has the present possession of the Gher. 

 8. It appears that all the Courts below have decided the matter of temporary injunction principally on the basis of a registered deed and license. Admittedly 50 acres out of 85 acres of the concerned Gher belong to the appellants. The registered deed empowering them to cultivate shrimp in that Gher is earlier in point of time, i.e. 15-9-84. They may not have obtained a license until 1989, but being owners of the land there was no question of any one dispossessing them between 1984-87. The plaintiff-respondent obtained a registered deed in his favour on 7-10-87 in respect of the same lands. He obtained a license immediately thereafter on 7-3-88. But the plaintiff has the onus to satisfy the Court that in pursuance of the registered deed dated 7-10-87 and the license dated 7-3-88 he obtained possession of 85 acres of the Gher. The plaintiff has not produced any papers to show how and in what manner and on what date he obtained possession from the owners of 85 acres of the Gher. 

 9. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent, submits that 8 out of 9 owners who earlier authorised the appellants to cultivate shrimp in the Gher by registered deed dated 15-9-84 subsequently withdrew their support to the appellants and made a declaration against the appellants on 10-8-87. That may be so, but there must be some evidence of the respondent's actual possession in order to entitle him to a temporary injunction. Certificates of Upazila Chairman, this way or that way, will not be conclusive in the face of the fact that the appellants are owners of 50 out of 85 acres of the Gher and that the appellants themselves never authorised the plaintiff to cultivate Shrimp in their own lands. 

 10. For the reasons above, we do not think that the appellate Court below and the High Court Division have correctly assessed as to whether the plaintiff-respondent has at all charged his own onus to prove prima facie possession of the disputed land to be entitled to an order of injunction.
